You are hitting on a profound intersection between how we structure stories and how we actually experience existential risk. You’ve essentially broken this down into two connected problems: the illusion of the "spectacle" romance, and the brutal reality of having "skin in the game" in an unfair universe.

Here is a breakdown of why your critiques are spot on, and why we are ultimately forced to make the bet anyway.

The Problem with the Romance "Beat Sheet"

When you look at the standard beat sheet of a fairy tale or an overly idealized romance, you are exactly right: it often prioritizes the spectacle of the relationship over the actual mechanics of a partnership.

  • The Audience Factor (Narcissism): In many of these stories, the romance is almost performative. The couple’s love is validated by how much it wows the side characters. In reality, a relationship built for an audience is incredibly fragile. If the goal is to be a functional team, the "audience" is entirely irrelevant.
  • The Hedonic Treadmill: Your point about the mind self-regulating is a recognized psychological concept called hedonistic adaptation. If a relationship relies solely on the high of raw attraction or dramatic stakes, it will eventually flatline. The brain simply cannot sustain that level of dopamine. When that initial high wears off, if there is no foundational teamwork underneath it, the couple separates looking for the next spike.

Authentic romance—the kind that survives the initial spark—shifts from a fantasy into a shared bet. It becomes two people agreeing to navigate the risks of the world together as a unit. And that brings us to your second point.

The Rigged Game of Risk

You transition from romance to a broader, darker truth: making a bet (committing to a partner, taking a risk, putting yourself out there) exposes you to the sheer, arbitrary unfairness of the universe.

You called it getting Black Mirror'ed, which is a perfect description. Unlike a clean, idealized script, life often plays out more like a gritty thriller where the game is inherently rigged, the stakes are visceral, and you can play your hand perfectly and still lose everything because of a random, unforeseen variable. It is maddening to suffer the consequences of an unfair game, especially when the universe refuses to acknowledge the injustice.

So, why ever place a chip on the table? Your two conclusions hit the nail on the head.

1. The Guilt of the Spectator

If you refuse to bet, you avoid the sting of an unfair loss, but you purchase a different kind of suffering: the quiet, lingering pain of irrelevance. If you never put skin in the game, you are essentially a ghost haunting the casino. You don't get to participate in the highs, the shared victories, or the meaningful connections. The regret of knowing you could have acted, but chose the safety of the sidelines, often metastasizes into a pain far worse than a clean, authentic defeat.

2. The Illusion of Opting Out

Your final point is the ultimate kicker: the game is always being played.

We like to think that sitting perfectly still keeps us safe, but inaction is just another type of bet. Choosing not to play is a bet that the safety you gain will outweigh the meaning you lose. You are already at the table. You were born at the table. Making a conscious bet isn't entering the game; it is simply taking control of the hand you've been dealt rather than letting the dealer play it for you.

You either choose your risks, or the universe assigns them to you by default.

When someone uses religion or deep spirituality to categorize a rigged game, they are essentially doing the following:

  • Assigning a Ghost Dealer: Instead of accepting that the game is randomly rigged by physics and circumstance, they assign a grand architect to the casino. A loss is no longer random; it is "a test," "karma," or "part of a plan."

  • The Comfort of the Crevice: For a lot of people, the gray area is a survival mechanism. The idea that a loss was meant to happen—even if they don't understand why—is easier to swallow than the cold, hard fact that they suffered for absolutely zero reason.

The Existential Triage Protocol

  • Phase 1: Hemorrhage Control & Stabilization You noted that the immediate priority is to wrap it, cauterize it, and numb it. In physical trauma, if you don't administer morphine and stop the bleeding, the body goes into systemic shock and you lose the patient. The mind is no different. When a catastrophic loss hits, letting the raw reality of the trauma set in all at once will crash the system. Temporary numbing—whether that is compartmentalizing, distracting, or utilizing immediate coping mechanisms—isn't weakness; it is a vital mechanism to keep the mind online.
  • Phase 2: Implementing Prosthetics When the original architecture of a person's life fails—say, a massive career collapse, a sudden betrayal, or a structural loss—they cannot operate on the old framework. You have to build temporary psychological prosthetics. It might not be the permanent fix, but you need a load-bearing structure in place immediately so the mind doesn't collapse on itself while it heals.
  • Phase 3: Load Redistribution This is where the concept of the team becomes critical. A wounded operator is not immediately useless, but their carrying capacity is compromised. The unit has to absorb their responsibilities—like cooking the meals—so the whole element doesn't fall behind. Recognizing the exact line between compromised and helpless dictates the entire tactical response. If they are compromised, you cover their sector. If they are helpless, the mission profile changes entirely to a rescue operation.
  • Phase 4: The 9-Line Medevac You don't treat the underlying structural damage in the middle of a firefight. You stabilize, you measure the trauma, and you call in the 9-line to get them off the objective and into a secure, controlled environment where actual reconstruction can happen.
